full_title: CHARLON FERNANDO Y ESMA, PETITIONER, VS. PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, RESPONDENT.
subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
syllabus_topic: VII. Criminal Procedure > M. New Trial or Reconsideration (Rule 121)
topics: Three requisites for a witness's retraction to be a ground for new trial
Recantations are generally unreliable but may justify new trial when the sole identifying witness recants under special circumstances
CA may receive evidence on new trial (Rule 124, Sec. 12; CA Internal Rules)
Relaxation of procedural rules when liberty is at stake
doctrine:
**For the retraction of a witness to be a ground for new trial, it must be shown that: (1) the retracting witness's trial testimony is essential to the judgment of conviction, so that its elimination would lead the trial judge to a different conclusion; (2) special circumstances exist which, coupled with the retraction, raise doubt as to the truth of the testimony given at trial; and (3) no other evidence sustains the judgment of conviction except that testimony.** The Court drew these requisites together from Reyes v. People (1941, En Banc) and People v. Manigbas (1960, En Banc). The ground is newly discovered evidence under Rule 121, Section 2(b): evidence discovered after trial, which could not have been discovered and produced at trial with reasonable diligence, and which is material and would probably change the judgment.

The general rule is reiterated: affidavits of recantation executed after conviction are "very unreliable," and merely impeaching evidence or retractions do not ordinarily justify a new trial. A new trial is warranted, however, where the sole eyewitness who identified the accused recants and the record shows special circumstances, such as suggestive identification, a complainant who suspected the accused beforehand, and a grudge between the families.

When a new trial on newly discovered evidence is granted in a criminal case on appeal, the CA may receive the evidence itself (Rule 124, Sec. 12; 2009 Internal Rules of the CA, Rule VI, Sec. 3(c)), so the Supreme Court remands to the CA. The Court may relax procedural rules in a Rule 45 petition when liberty is at stake and the petition has merit (Sanchez v. CA factors).
facts:
Charlon Fernando was charged with carnapping under RA 6539 for taking, on October 28, 2013 in Olongapo City, a blue Honda XRM motorcycle owned by Francisco Combate and valued at PHP 102,816.00. The only eyewitness was Darius Santos. He testified that at about 8:42 p.m. he saw Charlon pushing the motorcycle, that he and his friends told Charlon to kick-start it, and that Charlon then sped away. Two days later Darius described the man to Francisco, who "immediately recognized" him as Charlon. Francisco brought Darius to where Charlon was with three others, and Darius pointed to Charlon. Francisco testified that he did not see the taking and that his basis was that Charlon's group "have bad intention." Charlon's uncle testified to a long-time grudge between the families, and Francisco's own December 13, 2013 affidavit before the prosecutor reflected hostility toward Charlon's family. Charlon's defense was alibi: he was at his cousin's birthday party.

The RTC (March 30, 2017, Criminal Case No. 319-14) convicted Charlon of carnapping on the strength of Darius's testimony. The CA affirmed in toto (January 30, 2020 Decision, CA-G.R. CR No. 40276). Charlon then moved for new trial before the CA. He presented Darius's Salaysay ng Pag-urong dated March 2, 2020, in which Darius stated the following: he did not see Charlon take the motorcycle; the taker was one "alyas Balong Camisera," a feared local figure; his aunt and uncle, Joan and Francisco Combate, coached him to point to Charlon and told him not to reveal they were relatives; he was a minor then and easily influenced; he did not know Charlon before seeing him in court, where Francisco told him to stare at Charlon so he could identify him; and he later saw the motorcycle at the Combates' house in 2018.

The CA denied the motion (January 14, 2021 Resolution), reasoning that a mere retraction does not necessarily vitiate the original testimony if credible. Charlon filed a Rule 45 petition. The OSG argued that the petition failed to attach material portions of the record, raised factual issues, and relied on an affidavit of retraction executed after conviction, which has no probative value.
issues: Whether the petition should be dismissed for non-compliance with Rule 45.
Whether Darius's retraction warrants a new trial.
Which court should receive the evidence on new trial.
ruling:
**1. No; the rules were relaxed.** The Court may suspend its rules considering matters of life, liberty, honor, or property; special or compelling circumstances; the merits of the case; a cause not entirely attributable to the party's fault; the lack of any showing that the review is frivolous or dilatory; and the absence of unjust prejudice to the other party (Sanchez v. CA). Since petitioner stood to lose his liberty for a considerable time and the petition had merit, the Court relaxed the rules in the interest of substantial justice.

**2. Yes.** Under Rule 121, Section 2, a new trial may be granted for errors of law or irregularities, or for newly discovered evidence. Reyes v. People holds that retractions do not justify new trial "unless it is shown that there is no evidence sustaining the judgment of conviction except the testimony of the retracting witness." Manigbas warns that recantations after conviction are "very unreliable" and justify a new trial only if special circumstances, coupled with the retraction, raise doubt as to the trial testimony and that testimony is essential to the conviction. Combining these, the Court laid out the three requisites, and all were present.

(a) **Darius's testimony was essential.** He alone identified petitioner; "[w]ithout it, the prosecution would have had no leg to stand on." (b) **No other evidence sustained the conviction.** Francisco proved only his ownership, did not witness the taking, and relied on what Darius told him. (c) **Special circumstances raised doubt.** First, the retraction itself explained that Darius was a coached minor who identified the wrong man. Second, Francisco's testimony showed he suspected petitioner beforehand and brought Darius to petitioner's location to pick him out of four people, which shows "the suggestiveness of the identification." Third, the uncle's testimony on a long-time grudge was consistent with Francisco's December 13, 2013 affidavit. Given the gravity of the penalty for carnapping, a new trial "would better serve the ends of justice since it is better to liberate a guilty man than to unjustly keep in prison one whose guilt has not been proved."

**3. The Court of Appeals.** Under Rule VI, Section 3(c) of the 2009 Internal Rules of the CA, the CA may receive evidence in criminal appeals where a new trial is granted on newly discovered evidence, pursuant to Rule 124, Section 12. The case was remanded to the CA.
disposition: The petition was GRANTED. The CA's January 30, 2020 Decision and January 14, 2021 Resolution in CA-G.R. CR No. 40276 were REVERSED and SET ASIDE. The CA was DIRECTED to receive evidence and render a new decision as warranted by the whole evidence of record, and the records were REMANDED to the CA for that purpose.

bar_questions.q: Jomar was convicted of carnapping solely on the testimony of Kiko, who identified him as the man he saw riding away on the stolen motorcycle. The owner did not witness the taking. While Jomar's appeal was pending in the Court of Appeals, Kiko executed an affidavit retracting his testimony. He stated that the owner, his uncle, had pointed Jomar out to him before the police lineup and coached him on what to say, and that the real thief was another person whom he feared. The owner had admitted on the stand that he suspected Jomar even before Kiko described the thief. Jomar moves for new trial. The prosecution argues that recantations are unreliable. Should a new trial be granted?

alac.answer: Yes. Kiko's retraction, under these circumstances, is a valid ground for new trial on newly discovered evidence.
alac.legal_basis: Under Rule 121, Section 2(b), a new trial may be granted on newly discovered evidence. For the retraction of a witness to be a ground for new trial, three requisites must concur: (1) the retracting witness's testimony is essential to the conviction, so that its elimination would lead to a different conclusion; (2) special circumstances, coupled with the retraction, raise doubt as to the truth of the trial testimony; and (3) no other evidence sustains the conviction except that testimony. (Fernando v. People, G.R. No. 259589, July 29, 2025, drawing on Reyes v. People and People v. Manigbas)
alac.application: Kiko was the only witness who identified Jomar, so without his testimony the prosecution has no case, which satisfies the first and third requisites. The owner did not see the taking and only relayed suspicion. Special circumstances raise doubt about Kiko's trial testimony: the owner suspected Jomar beforehand and pointed him out to Kiko, which makes the identification suggestive, and Kiko explains he was coached by his own relative. Recantations are generally viewed with suspicion, but here they are coupled with circumstances already appearing in the record.
alac.conclusion: A new trial should be granted so that Kiko's retraction can be tested and weighed with the whole evidence.

bar_questions.q: Same facts, except that the stolen motorcycle was found in Jomar's garage two days after the taking, a CCTV recording shows Jomar riding it out of the owner's compound, and Kiko's affidavit of retraction merely states that he "is no longer sure" of his identification, without explaining why. Should a new trial be granted?

alac.answer: No. The retraction does not meet the requisites for a new trial.
alac.legal_basis: Affidavits of recantation executed after conviction are "very unreliable," and evidence that merely impeaches or retracts trial testimony is not a ground for new trial unless (1) the retracting witness's testimony is essential to the conviction, (2) special circumstances coupled with the retraction raise doubt as to its truth, and (3) no other evidence sustains the conviction. (Fernando v. People, G.R. No. 259589, July 29, 2025; People v. Manigbas; Reyes v. People)
alac.application: The conviction is supported by evidence independent of Kiko: the CCTV recording and the recovery of the motorcycle in Jomar's garage. Kiko's testimony is therefore not essential, and eliminating it would not lead to a different conclusion. His bare statement that he is "no longer sure," with no special circumstance casting doubt on his trial testimony, is the kind of retraction that would make a mockery of solemn trials if it were allowed to set aside a judgment.
alac.conclusion: The motion for new trial should be denied because the retraction is neither essential nor coupled with special circumstances, and other evidence sustains the conviction.

bar_questions.q: The Supreme Court, on a Rule 45 petition, finds that an accused-appellant is entitled to a new trial on newly discovered evidence, consisting of the sole eyewitness's affidavit of recantation, which was first presented to the Court of Appeals after it affirmed the conviction. (a) Must the case be remanded to the RTC for the new trial, or may the CA receive the evidence? (b) Can the Supreme Court entertain the petition despite the petitioner's failure to attach material portions of the record?

alac.answer: (a) The CA may receive the evidence, and the case may be remanded to the CA. (b) Yes. The Court may relax its procedural rules where the accused's liberty is at stake and the petition has merit.
alac.legal_basis: Under Rule VI, Section 3(c) of the 2009 Internal Rules of the Court of Appeals, the CA may receive evidence in appeals of criminal cases where a new trial is granted on the ground of newly discovered evidence, pursuant to Rule 124, Section 12. The Court may suspend its rules considering matters of life, liberty, honor, or property; special or compelling circumstances; the merits of the case; a cause not entirely attributable to the party's fault; the lack of any showing that the review is frivolous or dilatory; and the absence of unjust prejudice to the other party. (Fernando v. People, G.R. No. 259589, July 29, 2025, citing Sanchez v. Court of Appeals)
alac.application: Since the new trial is grounded on newly discovered evidence in a criminal appeal, the CA itself can take the recanting witness's testimony and render a new decision on the whole record, as the Supreme Court directed in Fernando. As to the procedural lapse, the accused faces long imprisonment and the petition shows merit, since the conviction rests on a single witness who has recanted under suspicious circumstances. These are the compelling reasons that justify relaxing the rules.
alac.conclusion: The case may be remanded to the CA to receive evidence and render a new decision, and the procedural defect does not bar the petition.

notes: The decision's summary of the CA Resolution reads that the CA "reluctantly finds [the recantation] to be sufficient ground for a new trial" but still denied the motion. This may be a typographical error for "insufficient." The digest describes only the CA's stated reason for denial. The petition also alleged grave abuse of discretion by the CA, but the Court resolved it as a Rule 45 petition on the merits of the new trial. The RTC imposed an indeterminate penalty under RA 6539; the Court did not rule on guilt or penalty, which are left to the CA after new trial.
